sources.headline: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
sources.text: Figure caption, Smoke appears after explosion heard in Iowa near Army detonation siteByAna FaguyUpdated 1 hour agoThe US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked widespread fears of health and environmental problems across the region.Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".President Donald Trump said reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations". Plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused multiple times before Wednesday's detonation following public outcry and legal challenges.Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising. "The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media."We are watching EPA's [Environmental Protection Agency] MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," he added.The explosives had been in storage for around 20 years, and degraded as part of a process known as recrystallisation - this made them more responsive to accidental detonation from friction or other movement.No level of lead exposure is considered safe, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to harmful effects.Image source, Sandy MabeusMiddletown Mayor Rodney Johnson told the BBC he felt "relieved" and "vindicated" after the detonation.He watched the blast from his job at a manufacturing plant eight miles (12km) away from the blast - and monitored a camera at his two-bedroom home just one mile from the detonation site. "We did not feel anything. We did not see anything," Johnson said.Also eight miles away from Middletown, Sandy Mabeus closed the windows and the garage at her home, brought their outdoor cat inside and hunkered down. The family watched three separate live streams on iPads and televisions of the explosion as it happened."We did not feel or hear a thing here," she told the BBC, adding that she checked the videos to confirm it had actually happened."The waiting and wondering has not been a good thing for anybody in the area," she said. "Hopefully they had a very good result and we can just get on with things."Iowa farmer David Vandenberg lives about 20 miles from the blast site and said he first learned of the detonation around two weeks ago. The Army Corps of Engineers took samples from his yard and pond on Tuesday."I was listening this morning, and I did hear a rumble about nine o'clock," he told the BBC on Wednesday, but didn't see or smell anything.Vandenberg expects officials to return to take more samples but "was happy to see that the blast was relatively contained. "I think the effects will be minimal"But there is also caution from some. Iowa's incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand said there was "more testing to do" and called for "immediate transparency" to explain why the lead-up was "so chaotic and unclear".Sand said that any Iowans who have been impacted in any way "must be taken care of fully, right away".Cameron Hamilton, administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), said there would be additional resources and testing in the coming days and weeks.In recent weeks, the US Army scheduled and rescheduled their detonation ahead of colder winter temperatures.It also warned locals of "potential exposure to toxic lead dust", which led to some panic. It instituted measures including an optional evacuation zone and a shelter-in-place advisory ahead of the detonation.The Army faced pushback from residents and politicians alike and there were legal challenges to prevent the detonation from going ahead on environmental and health grounds. But on Monday, the appeals court overturned a decision to halt the blast. It said that - while these concerns were valid - the risk from an unplanned explosion was greater.Sheila Flynn and Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu contributed to this report

sources.headline: US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
sources.text: Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far.United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Trump delays explosive detonation in US state of Iowa amid legal battleslist 2 of 4US army says detonation of lead explosives in Iowa will proceed Wednesdaylist 3 of 4US Army to detonate more than 4 tonnes of lead azide in Iowa on Wednesdaylist 4 of 4US Army detonates toxic lead explosives in Iowa amid health concernsend of listThe controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”‘Zero detection of airborne lead’Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

Iowa: Toxic dust fears as US Army blows up 10,000 pounds of explosives

Issued on: 25/11/2026 - 17:14

Share

An enormous explosion rang out across rural Iowa Tuesday as the US military carried out the controlled detonation of some 10,000 pounds of lead azide. US officials say the material, which was once used as a detonator in munitions, had become unstable and was at risk at risk of spontaneous explosion. But the risk of a toxic cloud of lead dust spreading out from the blast zone has caused public safety fears among locals.

US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears
Share
Comments
Add Euronews on Google
Copyright AP Photo
By Greta Ruffino
Published on 25 November 2026 - 18:55 GMT+1
The controlled explosion of five tonnes of hazardous material has raised concerns over lead pollution and its potential impact on public health and the environment.

The US Army destroyed the country's entire stockpile of lead azide at a military ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, amid concerns that the deteriorating explosives could spontaneously detonate as temperatures dropped.

ADVERTISEMENT

The controlled explosion has sparked fears among local residents and environmental groups over the potential release of toxic lead dust into the atmosphere.

Footage showed two white plumes rising from the site before quickly dissipating. Local schools cancelled classes, while some residents sealed their windows and doors as a precaution.

The chemicals, which are used in the production of munition, had been stored at the Iowa facility since 2009.

Hundreds of homes and farms at risk of lead contamination

An inspection in March revealed that the decades-old material had become increasingly unstable. Military experts concluded that a controlled explosion was safer than alternative disposal methods.

Administration building at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Austin Johnson)

Authorities urged residents living within an eight-kilometre radius of the ammunition plant to evacuate to avoid exposure to airborne lead particles.

Hundreds of homes and farms could be in the path of a toxic dust cloud containing lead. There is no safe level of lead exposure, with children and pregnant women particularly vulnerable to its harmful effects.

The army put protective barriers and other safety measures in place to limit the spread of hazardous particles into the surrounding environment.

Environmental groups fought to stop the explosion

The operation was rescheduled three times following public opposition and to allow for additional safety precautions and favourable weather conditions.

Environmental organisations launched legal action to prevent the explosion, but a federal appeals court gave the operation the green light on Monday, ruling that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had incorporated adequate safeguards to minimise lead dust dispersal.

Despite these assurances, residents remain concerned about the potential long-term consequences for their water supplies, agricultural land, animals and homes.

Transcript
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.
A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa.
Scott Olson/Getty Images
hide caption
Scott Olson/Getty Images
🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S. 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.
Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal. 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later. Today's listen
Tatyana Alanis for NPR
NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.
There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here. Life advice
Beck Harlan for NPR
If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth. 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title. For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more. 3 things to know before you go
Ezra Frech of Team United States competes during the Men's Long Jump T63 Final on three of the World Para Athletics Championships New Delhi 2025 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on Sept. 29, 2025 in New Delhi, India.

Dancing with the Stars wrapped up Season 35 last night, crowning Paralympian Ezra Frech and his partner, Daniella Karagach, as the winners of this year's Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time.Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.
